title: Land-use simulation & scenarios
text:
Theme 2 · Modeling integrated landscapes
How will a landscape look in coming decades under different land policies, farm management strategies, and climate conditions? I build spatially explicit land-use change models to explore these futures and the trade-offs among the services landscapes provide.
As a postdoctoral scholar at Penn State’s Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, I parameterized and calibrated a land-change model for an arid and semi-arid agropastoral system in southern Kenya, part of the NSF-funded project Towards regenerative landscape futures.
The work is guided by two ideas: that policies supporting flexible, heterogeneous land use sustain ecosystem services under stress better than policies that ‘harden’ landscape structure, and that landscapes structured at the scale of adaptive livelihoods are more likely to regenerate.

title: Land-use simulation & scenarios
text:
Key insights

Future land-use patterns reflect a complex interplay between rising demand for, and limited supply of, suitable agricultural land.
Simulations reveal spatial trade-offs among land uses and ecosystem services that differ across policy and climate scenarios.

title: Rainfall variability & drought
text:
Theme 1 · Mapping spatiotemporal patterns
Rainfall is the lifeblood of farming and pastoral systems, and shifts in its timing and reliability ripple through livelihoods and ecosystems. I characterize how rainfall and drought vary across multiple space and time scales to reveal where and when landscapes are most exposed.
In Kenya, I combined self-organizing maps with wavelet analysis to describe rainfall variability at annual, seasonal, and intra-seasonal scales. At Oak Ridge National Laboratory, I examined historical, near-term, and projected drought across the conterminous United States.

title: Rainfall variability & drought
text:
Key insights

Rainfall in the study region has become more variable at annual, seasonal, and intra-seasonal scales.
Extreme wet and dry events are becoming more frequent, with potential harm to crop and pasture systems.
Rainfall patterns are highly heterogeneous across space, so impacts are unevenly distributed across a landscape.

title: Land users’ perceptions of environmental change
text:
Theme 2 · Modeling integrated landscapes
Farmers and pastoralists experience climate change through their fields, herds, and livelihoods. Their perceptions embody local and Indigenous knowledge and shape how they respond, which makes them essential for designing locally relevant adaptation.
Working with colleagues at Maasai Mara University, I studied how agropastoral land users in southern Kenya perceive changes in rainfall and in crop and pasture productivity, and how these perceptions compare with observed data.

title: Land users’ perceptions of environmental change
text:
Key insights

Perceptions varied widely among land users, signaling that climate impacts are felt differently across households and livelihoods.
Perceptions did not always match observed climate and environmental data, yet they reflected real impacts on local livelihoods.
Incorporating human dimensions is critical for landscape-scale modeling and management.

title: Land-use & land-cover change
text:
Theme 1 · Mapping spatiotemporal patterns
Landscapes carry the imprint of past decisions. I use satellite imagery and classified historical aerial photographs to reconstruct how land use and land cover have changed, and to connect those changes to their social, political, and climatic drivers.
My early regional work across Eastern and Southern Africa found patchy, spatially varying losses and gains in forest and cropland that largely offset one another in net terms, and that showed little relationship to national-level rainfall and temperature trends, pointing instead to socioeconomic and policy drivers.
More recently, in the agropastoral landscape of Narok, Kenya, I traced how historical land policies continue to shape contemporary land-use patterns.

title: Land-use & land-cover change
text:
Key insights

Land-cover change reflects an interplay between historical land policies and competition among land uses for resources.
The landscape has become increasingly homogeneous, a shift with potential consequences for social-ecological resilience.
Land use closely tracks the uneven climate patterns that govern land productivity.

title: Climate risks to agriculture
text:
Theme 1 · Mapping spatiotemporal patterns
My earliest research used Earth observation and GIS to support climate-smart agriculture and food security, much of it as part of the SERVIR program, a NASA–USAID initiative that brings satellite data into decision-making.
A focus of this work was frost, which periodically damages Kenya’s highland tea plantations. I mapped frost risk in the Aberdare region, tested how well MODIS land surface temperature detects frost events, and statistically characterized frost zones in the Kenyan highlands.

title: Climate risks to agriculture
text:
Key insights

Satellite-derived land surface temperature can help identify frost events in tea-growing areas where ground observations are sparse.
Vulnerability to extreme weather varies considerably across space, reinforcing the need for landscape-level, place-based adaptation.

title: Kotikot
text:
Mapping change.Modeling futures.Building resilient landscapes.


I use geospatial science to understand how land use, governance, and a changing climate reshape landscapes, and to find pathways that help people and ecosystems adapt and thrive.


Explore my researchPublications










Susan Malaso Kotikot, PhD
Assistant Research Professor
Department of Geography, Sustainability, Community & Urban StudiesUniversity of Connecticut





About me
I am interested in understanding how environmental change, land-use decisions, and human activities shape landscapes and the communities that depend on them. My work combines remote sensing, geospatial analysis, spatial modeling, spatial statistics, and mixed method approaches to evaluate landscape dynamics, identify emerging risks and opportunities, and support evidence-based decision-making across conservation, natural resource management, climate adaptation, and land-use planning.
I have applied these approaches across diverse social-ecological systems, including rangelands, forests, coastal environments, agricultural landscapes, and urbanizing regions. I am particularly interested in translating complex spatial data into practical tools, scenarios, and insights that help organizations evaluate alternatives, anticipate future change, and make informed decisions under uncertainty.
I value collaboration with fellow researchers, practitioners, communities, government agencies, and nonprofit organizations, and I am committed to open, reproducible workflows and capacity building that increase the accessibility and impact of science.
I hold a PhD in Geography and Climate Science from Penn State (2023), an MS in Earth System Science from the University of Alabama in Huntsville, and a BS in Environmental Planning and Management from Kenyatta University. Before joining UConn, I was a postdoctoral scholar with Penn State’s Earth and Environmental Systems Institute and the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, and earlier a research associate at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.


Research Interests

  
    Land-Use & Land-Cover Change
    Mapping how landscapes change, and why, using satellite and historical aerial imagery.
  
    Climate Variability & Impacts
    Characterizing rainfall variability, drought, and climate risks to social-ecological systems.
  
    Landscape Ecology
    Pattern–process relationships, fragmentation, connectivity, and landscape heterogeneity.
  
    Social-Ecological Resilience
    How policy, governance, and land users' experiences shape adaptive capacity.
  
    Land-Use Modeling & Scenarios
    Simulating future landscapes under alternative policy, management, and climate pathways.
  
    Decision Support
    Open, reproducible geospatial tools for land and ecosystem managers.

title: Geospatial decision analysis
text:
Theme 3 · Transdisciplinary research for management
At Oak Ridge National Laboratory, I developed geospatial frameworks to support planning for critical infrastructure and climate adaptation.
Projects included a multicriteria decision analysis for the strategic placement of reserve generators in Puerto Rico, planning green infrastructure placement using projected precipitation, estimating household electricity demand for urban infrastructure planning in select African countries, and exploring nighttime satellite imagery (VIIRS Day/Night Band) for monitoring power recovery.

title: Geospatial decision analysis
text:
Key insights

Physical landscape attributes, socioeconomic conditions, and environmental factors jointly shape vulnerability, so siting decisions benefit from integrating all three.
Incorporating climate projections helps target infrastructure where future needs will be greatest.

title: Mangrove monitoring & decision support
text:
Theme 3 · Transdisciplinary research for management
Mangroves protect coastlines, store carbon, and support fisheries, yet managers in many regions lack consistent, current data on where mangroves are being lost or recovering.
As a graduate fellow with the Smithsonian’s Marine Conservation Lab, I led a team that built a mangrove monitoring tool for ecosystem managers in the Caribbean. I developed a Random Forest classification in Google Earth Engine using Sentinel-2 imagery to produce multitemporal mangrove-cover maps, and coordinated research activities including engagement with local stakeholders.
I also contributed to work documenting mangrove cover, change, and uncertainty in Panama using open-access data.

title: Mangrove monitoring & decision support
text:
Key insights

Freely available satellite data and cloud computing can give non-technical managers timely, easy-to-use information on mangrove change.
The study highlighted numerous threats to mangroves and the need for adaptive management to curb degradation.

title: Protected areas & human wellbeing
text:
Theme 3 · Transdisciplinary research for management
Do protected areas benefit the people who live alongside them? With the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, I am exploring how mangrove protected areas relate to ecosystem health and human wellbeing in coastal communities.
The project integrates household socioeconomic and health data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) program with mangrove vegetation change data. My role centers on data acquisition and processing, building automated workflows in R, and fitting and selecting multilevel statistical models.

title: Protected areas & human wellbeing
text:
Key insights

This work is ongoing; results will help guide conservation decisions that support both people and ecosystems.

title: Regenerative landscape design
text:
Theme 2 · Modeling integrated landscapes
Resilience is often framed as a system’s ability to recover after disturbance. Regenerative thinking goes further, asking how landscapes can be intentionally shaped to strengthen their health, adaptive capacity, and potential to renew themselves.
Using spatial indicators of heterogeneity, fragmentation, connectivity, and functional adjacency, I diagnose how landscapes reorganize under alternative land-tenure regimes and management strategies, and I heuristically ‘design’ alternative landscape structures to test which ones best support human and environmental wellbeing.

title: Regenerative landscape design
text:
Key insights

Group-based land governance tends to maintain more heterogeneous landscapes, with more forest patches and better connectivity.
Privatization tends to homogenize landscapes through cropland aggregation and the loss of small forest patches.
Targeted strategies, especially conserving small forest patches and enhancing connectivity corridors, yield the strongest gains under climatic stress, whereas broad bundled interventions can underperform because their spatial effects offset each other.

title: Research
text: I study the ways multifunctional landscapes (places that simultaneously support livelihoods, biodiversity, and ecosystem services) are reorganized by interactions among climate variability, disturbance, and human activity. My work combines multi-scale remote sensing, GIScience, spatial statistics, land-use modeling, and mixed methods, and is organized around three connected themes. Select VIEW on any card to read more about the related studies.

title: Research
section: Mapping spatiotemporal patterns of dynamic landscapes
text:
Mapping spatiotemporal patterns of dynamic landscapes
I map and analyze change in land use, land cover, and climate across space and time to understand how landscapes are changing, what drives those changes, and where impacts are felt most.

title: Research
section: Modeling integrated landscapes for social-ecological resilience
text:
Modeling integrated landscapes for social-ecological resilience
Land-use legacies can shape ecosystems for decades and spill over into other places. I combine social and biophysical data with spatially explicit models to understand the drivers and consequences of land use, and to explore futures under alternative policies and climates.

  
    Land Users' Perceptions
    How farmers and pastoralists experience changes in rainfall and productivity, and why it matters.View
  
    Land-Use Simulation & Scenarios
    Modeling multifunctional landscapes under alternative policy, management, and climate futures.View

    Using heterogeneity and connectivity to design landscapes that do more than bounce back.View

title: Research
text:
Transdisciplinary research for landscape management
A central goal of my work is to support adaptive, data-driven management. I work with stakeholders to build decision-support tools and evidence that managers and policymakers can use to monitor change and prioritize action.

  
    Mangrove Monitoring
    An open Earth Engine tool that helps coastal managers track mangrove loss, gain, and recovery.View
  
    Protected Areas & Wellbeing
    Linking mangrove protected areas to ecosystem health and the wellbeing of coastal communities.View
  
    Geospatial Decision Analysis
    Siting and planning critical infrastructure under a changing climate.View

title: Research
text:
Where my research is heading
Building on this foundation, my future work asks how, and at what scales, climate change alters pattern–process interactions in landscapes, and how compound disturbances and spatially uneven stresses push ecosystems onto new trajectories. I am especially interested in moving beyond “bouncing back” to ask how landscapes can be deliberately designed toward more desirable states, by strengthening heterogeneity, connectivity, and regenerative capacity, and by matching resource management to ecosystem dynamics.
